newsitem.title: UK: British motorways open, bomb alert closes station.
newsitem.headline: British motorways open, bomb alert closes station.

text.p: Major British motorways were reopened on Friday after 24 hours of traffic chaos triggered by telephoned bomb warnings and the discovery of two bombs thought to have been planted by Irish guerrillas.

But London commuters suffered hours of misery after a new bomb alert at King's Cross station in the heart of the capital. The station was closed for five hours on Friday afternoon after police received a call that a bomb had been planted there.
A police spokesman said they had carried out a controlled explosion on a suspect package, but no bomb had been found.
Train services to the north of London were disrupted and roads around the station were jammed for hours. "It was black for quite a long time out there," a spokesman said.

The new alert, which also briefly forced police to close Waterloo and Euston stations, came after key stretches of motorway in central England were shut down on Thursday morning following coded telephone calls to police warning of bombs.
Police finally gave the all-clear for the central English motorways to reopen on Friday after hunting for more bombs.
The alert cost industry millions, intensifying concern about the cost of deadlock in the Northern Ireland peace process.

Sinn Fein, the political wing of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), has been excluded from talks about bringing peace to the British-ruled province until IRA guerrillas fighting to end British rule of the province call a truce.
Prime Minister John Major, campaigning for Britain's May 1 general election, said the IRA appeared to be responsible for the two bombs police discovered.

"It was intended deliberately to cause trouble...It looks as though it was the IRA playing silly games," Major told reporters. The opposition Labour party, tipped by pollsters to win the election, joined Major in his condemnation.

No group has yet claimed responsibility for the bombs but coded telephone calls are the standard warning from the IRA. The movement ended a 17-month ceasefire in February last year and has since detonated several bombs on the mainland.

Last week the IRA caused major disruption to rail services by setting off two bombs at an important rail junction in the northwestern town of Wilmslow, apparently signalling the targetting at key transport links during the election campaign.
